hints: Differentiate $x=2t+\sin2t$ and use the chain rule on $y=\ln(1-\cos2t)$.
Form the quotient and factor $1+\cos2t$ and $1-\cos2t$ using half-angle identities.
Cancel carefully to reduce the expression to the reciprocal of $\sin2t$.
walkthrough:
Differentiate $y$ with respect to $t$ using the chain rule $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\ln(u) = \dfrac{u'}{u}$:
$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t} = \dfrac{-(-\sin 2t \cdot 2)}{1 - \cos 2t} = \dfrac{2\sin 2t}{1 - \cos 2t}$$

Multiply out the denominator using difference of two squares:
$$(1 - \cos 2t)(1 + \cos 2t) = 1 - \cos^2 2t$$

Apply the Pythagorean identity $1 - \cos^2 2t = \sin^2 2t$:
$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{\sin 2t}{\sin^2 2t} = \dfrac{1}{\sin 2t} = \operatorname{cosec} 2t$$
This completes the proof.
